bodyMarkdown:
## Before you start

Bar charts and line charts separately.

## The idea in plain language

Sometimes one picture carries two different kinds of number — say, bars for total sales in crores and a line for profit margin in percent. They cannot share one axis, so the chart grows a second one on the right.

The single most important habit here: check which axis each series belongs to before reading any value.

## What is actually going on

A combination chart mixes chart types precisely because the quantities are of different kinds — usually an absolute amount and a rate or percentage.

The left axis serves one series, the right axis the other. Reading a line against the bar axis produces confidently wrong answers, and the chart is often designed so that mistake yields one of the offered options.

The interesting questions ask you to combine the two: revenue from the bars times margin from the line gives profit, which appears nowhere on the chart directly.

## Every question type you will meet

Each of these is a shape a question in this topic actually comes in. Learn to recognise the shape first — in a timed paper, picking the right method is most of the battle, and the arithmetic is the easy part.

### 1. Matching each series to its axis

**Spot it when:** bars and a line on the same chart, usually with axes on both sides.

1. Identify which series belongs to the left axis and which to the right. The legend says so.
2. Never compare a bar's height to a line's height directly — they are on different scales.
3. Read each series against its own axis every time.

**Worked through:** A line below the bars can still represent a much larger number if its axis runs to 1000 and the bars' runs to 50.

### 2. Questions mixing both series

**Spot it when:** 'revenue per unit', where units are bars and revenue is the line.

1. Read both values against their correct axes.
2. Then do the arithmetic the question asks for.
3. Sanity check the units of the result.

**Worked through:** Revenue 600 (right axis) over 40 units (left axis) gives 15 per unit.

## Check yourself

You are ready to start practising this topic when you can:

- Assign each series to the correct axis before reading anything.
- Combine values from two series with different scales.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Bars show revenue of Rs. 200 crore and a line shows a profit margin of 15 percent for the same year. Find the profit.
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Profit $=$ revenue $\times$ margin $= 200 \times \dfrac{15}{100} = 30$ crore.

Neither axis showed profit directly — it had to be built from both series.

formulaCards.title: Two axes, two scales
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Identify which axis each series uses before reading anything. Bars and lines normally use opposite axes.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A line at '15' may mean 15 percent on the right axis, not 15 crore on the left.

formulaCards.title: Combining the series
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Absolute $\times$ rate gives a new absolute. This is usually what the hard question wants.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: Revenue 400 with margin 12 percent gives profit 48.

commonTraps: Reading a percentage line against the absolute axis.
Assuming both axes start at zero or share a scale.
Adding a percentage to an absolute value. They are different kinds of quantity.
